sentences.text: This creature was roughly the size of a modern chicken, featuring a lengthy skull packed with approximately ten teeth in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower jaw.
Its skeleton included a well-developed U-shaped furcula, commonly known as a wishbone, which supported its ability to walk effectively on the ground as well as fly.
The breastbone, or sternum, was elongated rather than wide to provide space for powerful flight muscles.
Its feet possessed long toes with elongated finger bones and relatively straight claw tips.
Some individuals retained long feathers on their lower limbs, creating an appearance of having four wings.
The species became infamous after parts of its fossil were used to construct the fraudulent specimen known as Archaeoraptor.
A later taxonomic review determined that the name Archaeovolans repatriatus was merely a duplicate, or junior synonym, of Yanornis.
The genus was formally named by Zhou and Zhang in the year 2001.
The type species, Yanornis martini, was described using multiple fossils recovered from the Jiufotang Formation near Chaoyang.
Scientists have documented a total of four distinct fossil occurrences for this genus.
Evidence from fossils containing fish remains within the stomach and crop indicates that this animal primarily consumed fish.
One individual was found holding a large quantity of stones, referred to as gastroliths, in the gizzard area.
Research suggests that its fish-eating habits and related physical traits represent convergent evolution with the distantly related enantiornithine bird Longipteryx.
The lack of a prefrontal bone and a non-diapsid skull structure place Yanornis within the ornithuromorph lineage.
In broader taxonomic terms, the animal is classified within the class Reptilia.
It belongs to the family Yanornithidae.
A study published in 2006 identified Yanornis, Yixianornis, and Songlingornis as forming a monophyletic group.
The order Yanornithiformes was established to separate Yanornis and its relatives from other early ornithurans such as Gansus.
Some researchers propose that the species Aberratiodontus wui is either a badly preserved example of Yanornis martini or a close relative.
Fossils of this animal have been discovered in Liaoning province, China, within the 120-million-year-old Jiufotang Formation and the 124-million-year-old Yixian Formation.
It lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, a period spanning from 125.77 to 113.2 million years ago.

It remains debated whether Yanornis could switch its diet between fish and seeds, as subsequent studies have questioned the hypothesis that the preserved stones were gastroliths used for grinding seeds.
